doc.title: Tommy Newsom and Ross Tompkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Growing up in the big band era
summary: Tommy was born in 1929 and grew up with standards and bands influenced by jazz; he was drawn to improvising.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Maybe get the bench to move or something. Yeah. Well that was really enjoyable. And can I take you guys back a little bit to why this kind of music? Why did you get into jazz and swing music?

That’s really hard to say. I grew up in, I was born in 1929. So I grew up during the big band era, and like pop music was, a lot of it was standards. Like you know the Gershwin tunes and Cole Porter and Jerome Kern and all that. And a lot of it was “The Three Little Fishes.”
Well Mel Powell says he grew up when popular music was good and good music was popular.
Not so with kids these days.

But jazz was part of the music. Jazz was part of the way the bands approached things. They were jazzed up and they were all influenced by jazz and I came in that way. I heard it and it attracted me and I loved the improvising and oddly enough I think people know when a soloist is making it, even if they have no idea what’s going on. There’s something that happens I guess, because look at all these people that show up at these festivals. I don’t think they have much of a clue, other than something strikes them. You know they don’t know the chords or anything that’s happening. They might know the tunes. But they know when it’s happening. And I think as a little kid I did too. You did too, didn’t you, Ross?
